text: Every CI and CD pipeline runs as some identity — a token, a service account, a runner. Least privilege means that identity can do exactly what its job requires and nothing else. We'll look at why the default token on most platforms is more powerful than it needs to be, why a short-lived federated credential beats a long-lived static key, and why a runner building a public pull request should never share infrastructure with one that deploys to production.

GitHub's automatic GITHUB_TOKEN, generated fresh per run, defaults to broad read-write access across contents, issues, and pull requests. Most jobs need almost none of that. Declare a permissions block explicitly, and anything not listed is denied, not just unused. A test-only job needs contents read and nothing more. The same logic applies to a dedicated cloud service account — scope its IAM role to the one bucket or namespace it touches, never a broad built-in role attached because it was faster at setup.

A static AWS key or service principal secret pasted into your CI platform's secret store is a long-lived bearer credential — whoever holds it can use it from anywhere until someone rotates it. OIDC federation replaces that: the CI platform presents a signed token asserting which workflow, repo, and event triggered the run, and the cloud provider issues a temporary, scoped session in response. The assumed role's own trust policy restricts which repository can even request it.

That difference matters most when something leaks. A static key copied out of a log or a compromised dependency keeps working until someone notices and rotates it — which can be days. A federated session expires in minutes and was already scoped to one specific workflow run, so the same leak has a far smaller blast radius by design, not by luck.

Self-hosted runners raise a specific risk: if a runner pool executes pull request workflows from public forks, an attacker's PR can run arbitrary code that inherits whatever secrets that runner's environment holds. If production deploy credentials live on the same pool, a malicious PR can reach them. The fix is separating trust boundaries — ephemeral runners with no production access for fork-triggered jobs, a separate locked-down pool for deploy jobs, and requiring approval before a first-time contributor's workflow executes at all.

Scoped tokens, short-lived sessions, and runners that respect trust boundaries — that's least privilege applied to the pipeline's own identities. Next lesson moves to the dependencies that pipeline pulls in: software bills of materials and supply chain basics, what actually goes into one, and why that inventory matters the day a dependency you rely on turns out to be vulnerable.
